In a nutshell, what do we find in this year's emissions monitoring report? Well, overall risks to meeting our emissions budgets are growing. While emissions have been falling, which is a great thing, the progress is fragile and the pace is going to need to more than double over the next few years. So that means government putting in place additional targeted policies within the next 12 to 24 months.

The good news is that there are more cost-effective options than even before, and many of the things that reduce emissions can also bring down costs and increase resilience for households and businesses. But there are barriers in the way of people accessing those benefits, and this is where policy can be targeted to help reduce those barriers.

So if we move on to the next slide, which is a quick recap on our role here. So of course, the commission gives independent evidence and advice, but we also have this independent monitoring role. And it is designed so government can make well-informed choices and Parliament has that transparency around the trade-offs and consequences of different choices.

And it is really designed to provide predictability and a level of stability through the transition so that businesses, communities, councils can act with confidence rather than holding back under uncertainty. This year's monitoring report is looking at the second and third emissions budgets, which are those five-year caps that are the stepping stones that take emissions down towards our 2050 target, and it's also an assessment of what's next to meeting our 2050 target.

So we provide these reports every year, and every year the government has three months to respond, and then outline how it intends to address the recommendations of the commission This is part of our broader work program. Earlier this year, we have also given advice on the annual settings of the desks.

We have provided the National Climate Change Risk Assessment, and we are about to, in a couple of weeks, provide the monitoring report on adaptation, which is our other monitoring role. The other piece of our work program that's probably relevant is that we have kicked off the process for re-updating our advice on the fourth emissions budget.

And this is in response to the change in the target in the act, which has triggered us to do a redo of the original advice we had about the fourth budget, and that's going to be due March next year. So that's still a few months away. And finally, just some of the broader context that we are conscious of in doing this piece of work.

New Zealand is increasingly feeling the impacts of climate and, of course, in the next session, we'll be talking about that with the national risk assessment. At the same time, we've got uncertainty increasing globally. On the other hand, we have low emissions technology increasingly available and affordable, and particularly solar batteries, heat pumps, and electric vehicles. So, pushing in a more optimistic direction on those fronts. And then finally, why monitoring matters.

Monitoring encourages action. We've got a similar setup to how a business manages a budget. Emissions budgets set out what we need to achieve, what we can spend. The regular checks allow that course correction, and we have to anticipate some course correction will be needed because there's always uncertainty. So by providing these reports, it creates the transparency and accountability that helps increase public trust in the overall system.

We did see in 2024 that net emissions continued to fall due to forest planted in earlier years that continued to remove carbon from the atmosphere at greater rates.

The second emissions budget is at significant risk, and it's now too late to plant additional forests in order to meet any shortfalls in that budget. So addressing those risks requires greater steps to reduce gross emissions in those periods to address those risks. As noted before, there have been some since the 1st of April, and we've noted those in the introduction chapter and the more significant ones in our findings. We also note that the ministry merger, the Maori Climate Platform's funding cycle ending, and the merger of Crown Research Institutes may also have implications for Maori-Crown relations and recognition of mātauranga Māori in decision-making that need to be considered in addition to their climate impacts.

We've recommended the government update its approach in these areas to ensure that projections remain robust. Biomass can also now be cheaper than coal or gas across the temperature range, including in those higher heat scenarios, and that's particularly the case if businesses have access to hog fuel or wood chip locally that can enable them to use that at low cost. Emissions in 2035 could be up to three megatons lower if we achieved faster decarbonization of non-transport energy through taking up opportunities like these.
